title: Third conditional
tagline: Imaginary pasts: what would have happened if things had been different.
why: Talking about regrets and imaginary pasts — what would have happened if things had been different — is a skill B1 Preliminary tests directly in the reading cloze and rewards in Writing Part 2, where a good story often needs a 'what if' moment. Mixing up the second and third conditional (now vs. an already-finished past) is one of the most common B1 mistakes.

hook.text: Mateo missed the bus again. Sofia: "If you'd left home at seven, you wouldn't have missed it!" Mateo: "I know... If I hadn't stayed up so late, I would have woken up on time."
hook.ask: Mateo is talking about a morning that is already finished. Which verb form comes after if, and which comes in the result? Is he talking about the present or the past?

diagrams.title: An imaginary past

marks.label: He didn't wake up on time

diagrams.caption: Both events are finished and imaginary — the third conditional never changes the present.

rows.label: Example
cells: If I had more time, I would help you.
If I had had more time, I would have helped you.

rows.label: Real or not
cells: imaginary in the past — a regret

diagrams.title: How to build the third conditional

steps.label: Add would have + past participle in the result
Use could have / might have for other results

diagrams.caption: We say I'd have in speech, but write would have in full in your exam answers.

head: Pattern
If-half
Result half
Meaning
rows: an imaginary result in the past
a possible or uncertain result in the past

examples.text: If I had studied harder, I would have passed the maths test.
examples.note: a regret — I didn't study, so I didn't pass

examples.text: If we had left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the bus.
examples.note: the real past: we left late and missed it

examples.text: If Nadia had checked the time, she would have been on time.
If it hadn't rained, the match would have continued.
examples.note: the weather changed what really happened

examples.text: If Mateo had brought his umbrella, he wouldn't have got wet.
examples.note: one small change, one different result

examples.text: If Liam hadn't lost his ticket, he would have watched the film.

use.point: could have and might have in the result

examples.text: If she had trained more, she could have won the race.
examples.note: a possible result, not a certain one

examples.text: If we had asked for help, we might have finished sooner.
examples.note: might have = maybe, less sure than would have

examples.text: If you had told me, I could have helped you.
examples.note: an offer that came too late

examples.text: The situation could have been much worse.
examples.note: could have + been — talking about danger that didn't happen

examples.text: What would you have done if you had seen the accident?
examples.note: a hypothetical question about the past

examples.text: If they hadn't practised, they wouldn't have played so well.
examples.note: double negative: neither thing happened for real

examples.text: Would you have forgiven him if he had apologised?

watch_out.wrong: If I would have studied, I would have passed.
watch_out.right: If I had studied, I would have passed.
watch_out.why: No would in the if-half — only had + past participle.

watch_out.wrong: If I had studied, I would pass the test.
watch_out.right: If I had studied, I would have passed the test.
watch_out.why: The result also needs have + participle, because it's about the past.

watch_out.wrong: If it hadn't rain, we would have played.
watch_out.right: If it hadn't rained, we would have played.
watch_out.why: Past participle after hadn't, not the base verb.

watch_out.wrong: If I had more time, I would have helped you yesterday.
watch_out.right: If I had had more time, I would have helped you yesterday.
watch_out.why: Both halves must stay in the same imaginary past — don't mix with the second conditional's if + past simple.

watch_out.wrong: I would of gone if you'd asked me.
watch_out.right: I would have gone if you'd asked me.
watch_out.why: It's would have, never would of — that's just how 'd have sounds when we speak fast.

l1.wrong: If I would have studied, I would have passed.
l1.right: If I had studied, I would have passed.
l1.why: Spanish si + hubiera translates to if + had (past perfect), never would have, in the if-half.

l1.es: Si hubiéramos salido antes, no habríamos perdido el bus.
l1.wrong: If we had left before, we hadn't missed the bus.
l1.right: If we had left earlier, we wouldn't have missed the bus.
l1.why: The result half needs would(n't) have + participle, not just the past perfect again.
Talking about an imaginary past danger needs could have + participle, not could be.

l1.es: Habría ido si me hubieras dicho.
l1.wrong: I would go if you had told me.
l1.right: I would have gone if you had told me.
l1.why: Both halves stay in the past — would have, not just would.

remember.trick: Both halves stay stuck in the past!
remember.tip: If you see had in the if-half, the result must have have have in it too: would have, could have or might have.

dialogue.title: The 7:15 bus
dialogue.context: Mateo arrives at school late again, and Sofia, Liam and Nadia tell him what he should have done.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: You're late again! If you'd left home at seven, you'd have caught the bus.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: I know, I know. If I hadn't stayed up so late, I would have woken up on time.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: My alarm didn't go off. If I had checked the battery, it wouldn't have died.

lines.speaker: Nadia
lines.text: If you had asked me, I could have called you at seven.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: That would have helped! Next time I'll ask.

lines.speaker: Sofia
lines.text: Honestly, if it hadn't happened three times this month, I wouldn't have said anything.

lines.speaker: Mateo
lines.text: Fair enough. It could have been worse, though — I could have missed the whole morning.

lines.speaker: Liam
lines.text: True. If you'd missed the whole morning, Miss Vega would have called your parents.

can_do: I can talk about regrets and imaginary pasts with if + had + past participle.
I can use would have, could have and might have to show how sure I am about an imaginary result.
I can tell the difference between the second conditional (now) and the third conditional (a finished past).
summary: Third conditional = an imaginary past: if + past perfect, would have + past participle.
It's for things that didn't really happen — regrets, criticism, or 'what if'.
could have and might have make the result less certain than would have.
Both halves stay in the past — never mix if + past simple with would have.
In speech we say I'd have, but write would have in full for your exam.
